definition: Game Theory is a branch of mathematics used to analyze how rational participants (players) make decisions in situations where each player's outcome depends on the choices of others; it is applied to model how generators bid into power auctions.
core_idea: Optimal generator bidding is forward-looking rather than purely reactive to the current price, because avoiding unnecessary shutdown/restart costs can justify taking a loss in one period to save startup costs later; Game Theory concepts (utility maximization, Nash Equilibrium) formalize this kind of multi-period, competitive decision-making.
key_points: A player's 'utility' is the benefit or loss they receive from playing the game; every player seeks to maximize their own utility.
A Nash Equilibrium is the stable pattern that results when all players' utility-maximizing decisions converge.
Optimal bidding strategies often incorporate predictions of future decisions (own and rivals'), not just a reaction to the current price, since restarting a shut-down steam turbine is costly.

Game Theory is often criticized as overly self-interested/harsh, but the author argues the real problem is usually that the 'game' itself was defined incorrectly (missing players or incentives), illustrated by a restaurant-tipping example where an unwitnessed-seeming interaction actually had an additional observer (the client).

Day-ahead and real-time power auctions are structured so that the equilibrium (optimal) bidding strategy for a generator is to bid its own true cost of production, and this is generally what is observed in practice.
relationships: Connects to unit commitment / thermal cycling economics (startup and shutdown costs).
Connects to day-ahead and real-time auction design.
trading_implications: A generator may rationally bid below its short-run marginal cost (take a loss) in some hours specifically to avoid a costly shutdown/restart cycle later.
Bidding strategy simulations that only look at current prices miss this dynamic; multi-period, game-theoretic reasoning is needed.
caveats: Assuming Game Theory always prescribes purely selfish, harsh behavior; in practice, poor outcomes often stem from mis-specifying who the real players/observers are, not from the framework itself.
